title: Nervous System
shortDescription: The brain's major regions, the spinal cord, and the central vs. peripheral divide that organizes the whole system.
genZNote: Your body's control center — one command HQ (CNS) and a nationwide wiring network (PNS).

illustration.alt: Labelled illustration of the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves
illustration.caption: Nervous System — Cellfie Human Anatomy

structures.name: Cerebrum
structures.description: The largest part of the brain, divided into four lobes.
structures.function: Reasoning, voluntary movement, sensory processing, personality.

structures.name: Cerebellum
structures.description: Smaller, densely-folded structure beneath the cerebrum.
structures.highYield: Often confused with the cerebrum by name — very different jobs.

structures.name: Brainstem
structures.description: Connects the brain to the spinal cord.
structures.function: Controls involuntary vital functions: breathing, heart rate, blood pressure.

structures.name: Spinal cord
structures.description: Long bundle of nerve tissue running through the vertebral column.
structures.function: Relays signals between the brain and the rest of the body; can trigger reflexes independently of the brain.

structures.name: Peripheral nerves
structures.description: Nerves branching outside the brain and spinal cord.
structures.function: Carry sensory signals to the CNS and motor signals from the CNS to the body.

comparisons.distinction: CNS = brain + spinal cord (the processing center); PNS = all nerves outside the CNS (carries signals to and from it).
Cerebrum handles thought and voluntary movement; cerebellum handles balance and coordination.
Sympathetic prepares the body for stress/action (fight-or-flight); parasympathetic calms the body and supports digestion/rest.

questions.prompt: In the labelled brain illustration, which structure is mainly responsible for balance and coordinated movement?
questions.explanation: The cerebellum, not the cerebrum, is primarily responsible for balance and coordinated movement.
optionNotes: Handles reasoning and voluntary movement initiation, not balance itself.
Controls involuntary vital functions like breathing and heart rate.
Relays signals and handles reflexes, not overall balance.

questions.prompt: Which nervous system division is the autonomic nervous system actually part of?
options: Neither — it is separate from both
questions.explanation: The autonomic nervous system is part of the PNS, even though it is regulated by the brain — a very commonly tested trap.
optionNotes: It is a subdivision of the PNS, not separate from it.
It's specifically part of the PNS.

questions.prompt: Which type of neuron carries signals TOWARD the central nervous system?
questions.explanation: Sensory (afferent) neurons carry signals toward the CNS; motor (efferent) neurons carry signals away from it.
optionNotes: Carries signals AWAY from the CNS, the opposite direction.
Interneurons connect neurons within the CNS, not the general afferent pathway.
“Reflex neuron” is not the standard term for this direction of signal.

sections.heading: Major Brain Regions
bullets: Cerebrum — the largest part; higher functions such as thought, voluntary movement, sensory processing, and language.
Cerebellum — coordinates balance, posture, and fine motor movement.
Brainstem — connects the brain to the spinal cord; controls vital automatic functions like breathing and heart rate.
Spinal cord — the main pathway carrying signals between the brain and the rest of the body; also handles reflexes directly.

rows: All nerves outside the brain and spinal cord
Carrying signals to and from the CNS
Sensory and motor nerves, autonomic nervous system

sections.heading: Neurons, Synapses, and Reflexes
bullets: Sensory (afferent) neurons — carry signals from the body toward the CNS.
Motor (efferent) neurons — carry signals from the CNS to muscles/glands.
Synapse — the junction where one neuron passes a signal to the next, usually via chemical neurotransmitters.
Reflex arc — a fast, automatic response (e.g. pulling a hand off something hot) that can act via the spinal cord alone, without waiting for the brain to process it first.

sections.heading: Autonomic Nervous System
sections.body: The autonomic nervous system controls involuntary functions (heart rate, digestion, breathing rate) and has two opposing branches: the sympathetic branch ("fight or flight", raises alertness and heart rate) and the parasympathetic branch ("rest and digest", calms the body down).

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: The nervous system is the body's control and communication network, split into the CNS (brain, spinal cord) and PNS (all other nerves).
keyFacts: Cerebrum handles higher thought; cerebellum handles balance/coordination; brainstem handles vital automatic functions.
CNS = brain + spinal cord; PNS = everything else (sensory + motor + autonomic nerves).
A reflex arc can bypass the brain, acting through the spinal cord for speed.
Sympathetic = fight or flight; parasympathetic = rest and digest.
commonConfusion: Cerebrum (thought, voluntary movement) is frequently confused with cerebellum (balance, coordination) — similar names, very different jobs.
Sensory neurons carry signals TO the CNS; motor neurons carry signals FROM the CNS — a commonly reversed pair.

highYieldFacts: The cerebellum, not the cerebrum, is primarily responsible for balance and coordinated movement.
A reflex arc can trigger a response through the spinal cord before the brain even registers the stimulus.
commonTraps: Don't place the autonomic nervous system entirely in the CNS — it is part of the PNS, though it's regulated by the brain.
Brainstem controls involuntary vital functions (breathing, heart rate) — don't confuse this with cerebrum's voluntary control.
mustRemember: CNS = brain + spinal cord. PNS = all nerves outside the CNS.
Afferent (sensory) = toward CNS; efferent (motor) = away from CNS.

confusedTerms.distinction: Sympathetic prepares the body for stress/action (fight-or-flight); parasympathetic calms the body and supports digestion/rest.
